Question No. 1
MIKE DAVIDSON (Green) ( 14:04) to the Minister of Local Government: Has he
received any advice that shows that the rates cap will result in no savings for some households?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON WATTS
items.text: I’ve received advice that
the amount an average household saves will depend on what their council would otherwise have
increased rates by, and how these rates are allocated. If a council is already close to or within the
cap, the average savings will, naturally, be modest. That shows that the cap is workable when
councils prioritise. But many ratepayers are facing double-digit increases. For example, under
Hamilton City Council’s 2024 to 2034 long-term plan, an average household was on track to pay
around $6,400 a year by 2034. With increases limited to 4 percent, that would be around $4,170,
saving about $15,800 over a 10-year period. That is meaningful savings.

items.speaker: Mike Davidson
items.text: Does he think a young family saving $34 a year under the rates cap would be
better or worse off once higher fees for pools, libraries, public transport, and car-parking are
included, given his view in a Cabinet paper that a rates cap will “incentivise greater use of user
charges”?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON WATTS
items.text: First and foremost, I encourage the member to—[Interruption]

items.speaker: SPEAKER
items.text: Just hold on—wait on. We’ll start that again.

items.speaker: Hon SIMON WATTS
items.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. First and foremost, I’d encourage the member
to read the bill in regards to rates capping. The cumulative effect of rates increases means that
over a five- or 10-year period, Kiwi households will have considerable savings as a result of that
cumulative effect being limited to 4 percent. Don’t forget the rates increases last year were 14
percent on average across New Zealand; this year, 9 percent—4 percent with respect to savings.
What I also reflect is that not having a cap will not protect Kiwi ratepayers. Not having a cap will
also not protect them against those double-digit rate increases, and that is not the policy of this
Government.

items.speaker: Mike Davidson
items.text: How does he reconcile his claim that households will save money, with the
Ministry for the Environment’s feedback that “reduced rates revenue may be offset by increased
fees for services such as swimming pool entry, library fines, and parking. This could result in no
net savings for many households.”?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON WATTS
items.text: Well, on this side of the House, we understand the concept of
prioritisation and making decisions in regards to spending that is within a limit. We don’t have a
credit card without a limit on this side of the House, by any stretch. Councils will, and should,
prioritise their spending, like every single Kiwi household and business in this country. I make no
apology for councils needing to do that. Putting a limit on their increase of expenditure is a
sensible and pragmatic thing to do to protect Kiwi households.

items.speaker: Mike Davidson
items.text: Does he accept that including water services investment, which is exempt from
the rates cap, in his figures for Waitaki District Council in his answer to oral questions on 25
August artificially inflated his claims of savings by nearly 80 percent?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON WATTS
items.text: No, because what I was providing there was an example of how much
an average bill would increase—the differential between the average of 14 percent or 9 percent
versus 4 percent. Basic maths would indicate to the member that when you increase cumulative
bills by 14 percent or 9 percent, it is a heck of a lot bigger over a period of five or 10 years than
at 4 percent. On this side of the House, we are on the side of Kiwi ratepayers. We want to protect
Kiwi ratepayers from unreasonable, rollercoaster rates increases. That’s what we’re doing; we
make no apologies for that. That side of the House has no plan to protect Kiwi ratepayers.

items.speaker: Mike Davidson
items.text: Is it correct that the biggest savings from his rates cap will go to owners of
multimillion-dollar houses and holiday homes who don’t need support, while struggling families
may only save as little as $34 a year, only to face higher costs from reduced local services?

items.speaker: SPEAKER
items.text: A concise answer would be good.

items.speaker: Hon SIMON WATTS
items.text: No.

Question No. 2
DAN BIDOIS (National—Northcote) ( 14:09) to the Minister of Revenue: Is the
Government considering a capital gains tax on properties used for both residential and business
purposes?
Hon SIMON WATTS (Minister of Revenue) ( 14:09): No, this Government will not
introduce a capital gains tax on the family home or on small businesses. For many Kiwis, the line
between the two isn’t so simple. They might live in the front of a property and run their business
from a workshop, garage, or an office out the back. We won’t punish people for using their own
homes to build a business and get ahead. We’re on the side of Kiwis that work hard, doing the
right thing and wanting to get ahead.

items.speaker: Dan Bidois
items.text: Why do some New Zealanders choose to operate their business from the same
property they live in?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON WATTS
items.text: Because, for many small-business owners, it is the most practical and
affordable way for them to operate. A builder, for example, might keep their tools and equipment
at home. A mechanic might have a workshop on their property, or an entrepreneur couple might
lease out their house as an airbnb during the summer break. These are ordinary Kiwis, using
what they have to build something for themselves and their family.

items.speaker: Dan Bidois
items.text: What could a capital gains tax mean for a tradie or other small-business owner who
operates their business from their family property?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON WATTS
items.text: It could mean being taxed 28 percent on part of their family property,
simply because they have used it to earn a living. That means that a Kiwi who has worked hard,
paid their mortgage, and built a business from home could face a big tax bill when they sell or are
due to retire. That is the wrong message. It punishes aspiration, rather than rewarding it. On this
side of the House, we back people who work hard, invest, and take risks, and we do that and we
say: no new taxes.
Question No. 3
Hon CARMEL SEPULONI (Deputy Leader—Labour) ( 14:11) to the Minister for

items.speaker: Social Development and Employment
items.text: Does she stand by all her statements and actions?

items.speaker: Hon LOUISE UPSTON
items.role: Minister for Social Development and Employment

items.text: Yes, in the context in which they were given.

items.speaker: Hon Carmel Sepuloni
items.text: Why, when 36,000 fifteen- to nineteen-year-olds are not in work,
education, or training, did she cut the access to jobseeker payments of 18- and 19-year-olds?

items.speaker: Hon LOUISE UPSTON
items.text: Because our Government is clear: we want 18- and 19-year-olds in
education, training, or employment, and if they’re not, we expect that their families do support
them. We know that going on welfare is a trap. If a young person goes onto the jobseeker benefit
under the age of 20, on average they will spend another 21 years of their life on welfare. Our side
of the House is more aspirational for young people, and wants more for their futures.

items.speaker: Hon Carmel Sepuloni
items.text: How can she say she is supporting young people into work, when in
this term, she has cut off their access to a benefit while also limiting non-beneficiaries’ access to
employment support programmes?

items.speaker: Hon LOUISE UPSTON
items.text: I refute that. We now have 4,000 young people in job coaching,
which is a very intensive programme. We’re also incentivising those young people who then go
into employment and stay in a job for 12 months with a $1,000 bonus. We are doing things
differently. We want to release young people from the trap that they would otherwise fall into if
those guys were still in office. We want more for them.

items.text: Has she been advised if the Ministry of Social Development is

items.text: Is it the Minister’s view that it is better for a young person to owe money

items.text: As I said at the start, we believe that young people should be in
employment, education, or training, or supported by their families. If you look at comparable
countries, in Australia, there is a parental income test up to the age of 22; in France, you’ve got

items.speaker: Hon Willow-Jean Prime
items.text: This is New Zealand. You’re the Minister in New Zealand.

items.speaker: Hon LOUISE UPSTON
items.text: Well, we normally compare ourselves to Australia. I’ve just said it’s

items.text: Good, that’s enough. Just completely calm down.

items.text: You’re just making it up now.

items.speaker: SPEAKER
items.text: I beg your pardon?

items.speaker: Hon Carmel Sepuloni
items.text: Why does she refuse to acknowledge that at a time of rising

items.speaker: Hon LOUISE UPSTON
items.text: Very simply: because our side of the House knows that growing the

because we’re fixing the basics, and building the future for young New Zealanders. [Interruption]

items.speaker: SPEAKER
items.text: That general barrage like that has to stop. It’s the last question like that.

Question No. 4
SUZE REDMAYNE (National—Rangitīkei) ( 14:17) to the Minister of Revenue: Is the
Government considering introducing an inheritance or gift tax?
Hon SIMON WATTS (Minister of Revenue) ( 14:17): No, this Government will not
introduce an inheritance or gift tax. New Zealanders work hard, save, and invest so that they can
build a better future for themselves and their families. This Government backs aspiration, and we
will not be waiting at the end with another tax. [Interruption]

items.speaker: SPEAKER
items.text: Just a moment. I made the point before that when a question is being asked, no
one else speaks, and when a Minister is answering a question, he doesn’t need his colleagues to
assist him—or her.

items.speaker: Suze Redmayne
items.text: What types of New Zealanders could be affected by an inheritance or gift tax?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON WATTS
items.text: All New Zealanders who have worked hard will build up assets over
their lifetime. An inheritance tax could tax a home; a small business; people with a farm, savings,
investments, or other assets they want to pass on to their children. These are everyday New
Zealanders who have spent decades building something up for themselves and their families. In
what may already be one of the hardest moments in someone’s life—having just lost a parent or
a loved one—the last thing a family should face is an inheritance tax bill from the Government.

items.speaker: Suze Redmayne
items.text: What impact could an inheritance or gift tax have on New Zealanders’
incentives to save, invest, and build something for the next generation? [Interruption]

items.speaker: SPEAKER
items.text: Is somebody else wanting to answer the question?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON WATTS
items.text: It sends a chilling message to hard-working Kiwis. Instead, on this side
of the House, we want New Zealanders to save, to invest, to build businesses and create wealth
for themselves and their children. Layering new taxes on people who do these things would
discourage investment, hold back growth, and make it harder for Kiwi families to get ahead. That
is not what we stand for on this side of the House. Our focus is on fixing the basics, building the
future, and no new taxes.

Question No. 6

items.speaker: Development and Employment
items.text: What are the terms of reference, if any, of the review of the
wrongful benefit suspensions, and will the review consider compensation?

items.speaker: Hon LOUISE UPSTON
items.role: Minister for Social Development and Employment

items.text: I have made it clear to the Ministry of Social Development (MSD) that the review will consider the

who has been affected in operationalising mandatory reviews and any further actions that may
be needed to prevent these issues happening again. As I’ve already made clear in the House, I
will wait for the findings of the review on 10 September.
Ricardo Menéndez March: Does she acknowledge that supported living payment recipients
were captured by mandatory reviews, which ended up leading to processing delays, meaning that

items.text: As I’ve already said, the suspension of payments that was made

those payments were reinstated and backdated at pace.
Ricardo Menéndez March:  If she recognises the impact this could have had on people,

items.text: Well, as I’ve said, I will wait for the findings of the review.

back payments, as that cannot make up for potential debt or harm or worsening health outcomes
that people may have experienced due to missed payments?

items.speaker: Hon LOUISE UPSTON
items.text: As I said, the review will cover many components, including who has
been affected, and that’s why I’m waiting for that review.

Question No. 7
CATHERINE WEDD (National—Tukituki) ( 14:25) to the Minister for Tourism and

items.speaker: Hospitality
items.text: What recent progress has she seen on tourism in New Zealand?
Hon LOUISE UPSTON (Minister for Tourism and Hospitality) ( 14:25): Recent data
from Statistics New Zealand shows New Zealand’s international visitor numbers continue to climb.
Over 201,000 international visitors arrived in New Zealand in June 2026, which is up 8.1 percent
on June 2025. That puts international visitor arrivals for June at 95 percent of the 2019 levels for
the same period. Growing tourism is a key part of our Government’s plan to fix the basics and
build the future. This progress shows that our plan to grow the economy is working.

items.speaker: Catherine Wedd
items.text: What markets are seeing the strongest growth?

items.speaker: Hon LOUISE UPSTON
items.text: We are seeing continued growth from our largest visitor market—
Australia—with 108,200 arrivals, which is up 14 percent from last June. There was also strong
growth from other key tourism markets, including from China, with visitor arrivals reaching 14,300,
which is up 27 percent compared to June last year. Close to 200,000 cruise ship passengers are
also expected to arrive in New Zealand this season, with the launch at the weekend of the cruise
season. We are seeing the flow on of growth and confidence in our tourism and hospitality sector
as more visitors choose New Zealand as their next holiday destination.

items.speaker: Catherine Wedd
items.text: What steps is the Government taking to support progress in tourism growth?

items.speaker: Hon LOUISE UPSTON
items.text: We know domestic visitors generate nearly twice as many guest
nights as international visitors and account for around two-thirds of all guest nights across New
Zealand. We do not believe that New Zealanders booking a weekend away or travelling for a
family funeral, or a sports team travelling for a game should face an additional tax on top of the
costs they already pay when travelling domestically. That’s why we don’t believe in a bed tax and
we are working hard to attract more tourists to New Zealand, because the more visitors we have
in our cities and regions, the more money is being spent in shops and cafes. It’s a key part of our
plan to grow the economy so that we can keep investing in the front-line public services Kiwis rely
on, without having to reach for new taxes.
HEALTH
Question No. 8
Hon Dr AYESHA VERRALL (Labour) ( 14:27) to the Minister of Health: Does he
stand by his statement that “A sustainable health system relies on a steady pipeline of skilled New
Zealand-trained nurses entering the workforce”; if so, why?
Hon MATT DOOCEY (Associate Minister of Health) (14:28) on behalf of the Minister
of Health: Yes, in the context it was made. As the member will be aware, more than 2,100
additional nurses, on a net basis, have been employed by Health New Zealand since 2023, which
equates to a net increase of 1,640 fulltime-equivalents. The Government remains focused on
building on this track record so that we can continue to reduce wait times for patients and build
the future of our healthcare system. That is why, as at 14 August, there were 2,378 fulltime-
equivalent nursing roles actively being recruited across Health New Zealand, including 475
nurses who have accepted offers, with thousands more progressing through recruitment.

items.speaker: Tangi Utikere
items.text: Why have emergency department staff in Palmerston North had to resort to
begging Health New Zealand to send urgent help after he cut the number of nurses by 25 over
the past two years?

items.speaker: Hon MATT DOOCEY
items.text: Well, clearly, from my primary answer, that is incorrect, and what I
would point to is putting a wrecking ball to the health system in the middle of a pandemic,
centralising the health system, and taking away local decision-making. That member’s question
reinforces why, on 1 July, we brought back local decision-making for budgets, service delivery,
and recruitment decisions.
